title: Sparse Event Detection via Adaptive Context-Detail Gating
one_liner: A gating switch that only focuses on small moments of interest in long medical recordings.
lead: In a healthcare recording (heart rhythm, mood, activity), most of the data is boring silence. A few seconds matter: a heartbeat skip, a mood shift, a fall. The challenge is spotting these tiny needles in a huge haystack without getting distracted by normal variations. This paper adds a smart gate that says look-here-now or ignore-this, turning a generic detector into one that excels on sparse events.

problem.h2: Spotting rare moments in long recordings
paras: A patient's heart-rate strip runs for hours. Maybe two or three seconds contain an arrhythmia (an irregular beat). The rest is normal. A machine learning model, asked to find arrhythmias, faces a problem: it can study the entire recording, but it wastes effort on the 99% of boring normal sections, and its gradual learning gets diluted. A naive approach trains a detector on every single second equally; it gets confused by which clues matter.

Even detection transformers (models that excel at finding object positions in images, adapted here to find event moments in time) struggle: they treat every time-step the same, spread their focus evenly, and fail to concentrate when events are rare and spread far apart.

callout.html: Use a gate that turns on a detailed inspector only when the global scan says an event is likely. The reason this works: turning off detail on normal sections means the model never learns to recognize silence patterns, so its learning budget (the finite number of weight nudges during training) all goes to refining event recognition.

steps.text: Scan the entire recording at low resolution to spot rough regions.
Convert the labels (event yes/no, where it starts) into gating signals.
A learned module uses the signals to decide where to apply detail.
High-resolution inspector operates only at gated-open locations.
Precise event boundary and type from the detailed features.

paras: The paper adds a learnable gate module that sits between a global coarse scanner and a local fine-detail inspector. This gate uses information about event labels (transformed into numeric signals) to decide when the detail work is worth doing.
object.object: Gating signal from labels to detail outputs

hidden.h2: The gating signal: where should detail look?
hidden.name: Adaptive gate signal strength
paras: The hidden quantity is a learned gate signal—a numeric score at each time position that says how likely an event is present, built from transformed label information. It acts as a spotlight: zero means ignore this moment, one means zoom in here.

The paper learns this gate from the labels themselves (which time-steps are events, where events start). The gate learns to open only where past data says events live, so the expensive detailed detector runs only on the likely spots. This is opposite to treating every position equally.

heat.caption: Darker means gate is open, detail inspector is active. Learned to match event regions.

reads.html: The gate is a score at each moment that says how confident the model is that an event is happening right now. High gate score means use detail; low means skip.

The adaptive gating module uses transformed label embeddings (event presence encoding, temporal position encoding) to compute a learned gating signal that modulates whether fine-grained feature extraction is applied.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: coarse-to-fine with learned routing
paras: In a sparse setting, noise is your enemy. If the model tries to extract fine detail everywhere, it extracts detail from boring normal sections too, and that noise mixes with real event signals. Result: the model gets confused.

The paper's insight: use a coarse, fast scan to make a rough map of where events plausibly live. Then use that map to open a gate, so the expensive detailed inspector only runs at the likely spots. The gate is learned from label information—the paper shows it what events look like. After training, the gate learned to open near real events and stay closed in quiet sections.

This reduces noise because detail is not computed on noise—if you never compute features on normal silence, those features never confuse the model. It also saves compute: you do not pay the cost of detail on 99% of the data because the gate turns it off. And critically, it focuses learning: during training, the learning signals (gradients, or nudges to move weights in the right direction) flow through the detail detector only where there are real events. Fewer different pieces of the model get trained, so each piece gets stronger training on events rather than weaker training spread across both events and silence.

math.words: The gating signal at each position is learned as a function of transformed label embeddings, then used to weight the detail feature activations.
math.equation:
gate_t = sigmoid(W_gate * [label_presence(t), label_position(t)])
detail_active_t = gate_t * detail_features_t
symbols: the gate score (0 to 1) at time-step t, learned from training
a number: 1 if an event exists near t, 0 otherwise
a number: where in the event (start, middle, end); helps the gate learn the moment
learned weights that map label signals to gate scores
a smooth curve that squashes any number into a 0-to-1 score
the expensive high-resolution features at position t
the features actually used (zero if gate is closed, full if open)

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Time-step t=50 has an arrhythmia label: label_presence = 1.0, label_position = 0.5 (mid-event).
Gate input: [1.0, 0.5]. Weights W_gate multiply and add: W_gate[0] * 1.0 + W_gate[1] * 0.5 = 0.8 * 1.0 + 0.3 * 0.5 = 0.8 + 0.15 = 0.95.
Sigmoid(0.95) ≈ 0.72: the gate is mostly open.
Time-step t=60 is normal silence: label_presence = 0.0, label_position = 0 (no event).
Sigmoid(0.0) = 0.5: the gate is half-closed (learned to default down in quiet).
Detail features at t=50 are multiplied by 0.72, detail at t=60 by 0.5: the arrhythmia moment gets more weight.

math.note: The gate multiplies the detailed features by a learned score, so features are zeroed out when the gate is closed and kept when open.

charts.title: Naive detector (treats every moment equally)
charts.note: Without gating, detail is computed everywhere, confusing the model and wasting compute.

charts.title: This paper (gated detail)
charts.note: Gating focuses learning on event regions, reduces noise, and saves 65% of compute by skipping detail on silent sections.

items.b: Gate learns the wrong spots to look.
items.html: If the label signals are bad or the gate module is too weak, it may open at normal moments and close at real events, defeating the purpose. Fix: make sure labels are accurate and the gate has enough capacity to learn.
If the global scanner gives false maps, the gate's spotlight points to the wrong places. The detail inspector then refines noise. Fix: ensure the coarse pass is accurate on its own.

The gate learns from training labels but must generalize to new recordings. If the model fits the training label patterns too tightly, the gate fails on new data. Fix: use regularization and validate on held-out data.

The gate is a learned router that brings coarse and fine detectors into alignment: coarse points the way, gate selects, fine delivers precision. The three parts together beat either one alone on sparse events.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small synthetic dataset: a time-series of 1000 steps, mostly noise, with 5-10 true events (arrhythmias or mood shifts) scattered in. Train a baseline DETR (no gate) and a gated DETR (this paper's method) on half the data. On the held-out half, measure: how many events did each detect? How many false alarms in quiet sections? How much compute did each use (count feature extractions)? The gate should find more events, raise fewer false alarms, and use less compute because it skips work on quiet sections.
demo.closing: The demo must show that gating improves detection, cuts false alarms, and cuts compute all at once—because the gate focuses learning on real events so the model trains on signal not noise, and the gate turns off detail on silent sections so compute is saved without sacrificing accuracy.
